topic: The Ghost Army: the U.S. Army's 23rd Headquarters Special Troops and 3133rd Signal Service Company, the World War II deception units that used inflatable decoys, recorded sound, fake radio traffic and impersonation against German forces (1944-1945)
why_suitable: The topic is well documented by authoritative sources. Congress made detailed findings about it in Public Law 117-85 (govinfo.gov, 2022). The National WWII Museum has curated articles and a traveling exhibition. U.S. Army public affairs (army.mil) has published pieces on it, and the Speaker of the House press office issued a release for the 2024 Congressional Gold Medal ceremony. The Library of Congress holds a Veterans History Project interview, the U.S. Mint issued a bronze medal, and the Government of Luxembourg has issued a press release. A primary source exists in the unit's official history (Capt. Fred Fox, September 1945, National Archives RG 407). For viewers aged 50+, the story has strong human interest: art students and future famous designers fighting with rubber tanks and loudspeakers, a secret kept for about 50 years, and very old veterans receiving the Congressional Gold Medal in 2024. It has clear visual hooks (inflatable tanks, soldiers' sketches, medal design) and a natural chronology from Normandy to the Rhine. Some points are contested and must be labelled on screen: the number of operations, the declassification date, and especially the 15,000-30,000 'lives saved' figure, which has no traceable primary study.

claims.claim: 'Ghost Army' is the popular name for two U.S. Army units of World War II: the 23rd Headquarters Special Troops and the 3133rd Signal Service Company. Congress used the nickname in the title of the law awarding them the Congressional Gold Medal.
claims.notes: The law's long title calls them 'popularly known as the Ghost Army'. Strictly, the nickname is postwar or popular rather than an official designation.

claims.claim: The 23rd Headquarters Special Troops was activated on January 20, 1944.
claims.notes: Consistent across museum, Army and primary-document sources.

claims.claim: The unit was activated at Camp Forrest, Tennessee, under Col. Harry L. Reeder, who commanded it for the rest of the war.
claims.notes: The Kelly Foundation chronology (S15) also places the 603rd's move to Camp Forrest in January 1944.

claims.claim: Ralph Ingersoll, who worked with the British on deception planning for Operation Fortitude, proposed a U.S. unit dedicated to deception.
claims.notes: Single authoritative source (National WWII Museum curator). Wording should stay close to 'proposed' or 'conceived'.

claims.claim: The 23rd's authorized strength was 82 officers and 1,023 enlisted men, usually rounded to about 1,100.
claims.notes: PL 117-85 gives no total headcount.

claims.claim: The 23rd combined a headquarters company, the 603rd Engineer Camouflage Battalion (visual deception), the Signal Company Special (radio deception, formerly the 244th Signal Company), the 3132nd Signal Service Company (sonic deception) and the 406th Engineer Combat Company (security and engineering).
claims.notes: The findings in PL 117-85 list the HQ company, 603d, 406th and 3132d. The Signal Company Special appears in the museum and Legacy Project accounts.

claims.claim: Approximate component strengths: 603rd about 379 men, Signal Company Special about 296-300, 3132nd about 145, 406th about 168.
claims.notes: Minor variance (296 vs 'roughly 300'). The listed components total about 988; the rest of the roughly 1,100 is presumably headquarters and attached personnel. That last point is not stated explicitly.

claims.claim: The sonic deception companies (3132nd and 3133rd Signal Service Companies) were activated and trained at the Army Experimental Station at Pine Camp, New York (today Fort Drum), in 1944.
claims.notes: The months differ. PL 117-85 says March and June 1944 respectively; the Fort Drum article says both in March 1944.

claims.claim: Congress described the 3132nd and 3133rd as the only U.S. 'sonic deception' ground combat units of World War II.
claims.notes: This is a congressional finding. Present it as 'Congress called them...' rather than independent verification.

claims.claim: Sonic deception equipment was developed with Bell Labs, and civilian advisers helped train the troops. Soundtracks were recorded on magnetic wire recorders and played through powerful speaker systems mounted on vehicles, with separate tracks for vehicles, personnel and ambient sound.
claims.notes: The Fort Drum article mentions an M-10 tank destroyer fitted with sonic equipment; the museum mentions half-tracks.

claims.claim: The broadcast sound could be heard up to about 15 miles away.
claims.notes: Commonly repeated, but found only in the museum article here. Range would depend on weather and terrain (S9 says these factors governed volume). Say 'up to' or 'reportedly'.

claims.claim: A mobile weather station, mounted on a jeep, was used to adjust sound projection to conditions.
Visual deception used inflatable rubber decoys of tanks, artillery, trucks and aircraft to simulate larger forces.
Some inflatable decoys were manufactured by U.S. Rubber and Goodyear.
claims.notes: Stated in a photo caption in the museum article. Use a hedged phrase such as 'among the makers'.

claims.claim: 'Spoof radio' operators created phony radio networks and impersonated real units' operators. Some telegraphers could imitate an individual operator's Morse-code 'fist' (sending style).

'Special effects' (also called 'atmosphere') included counterfeit shoulder patches, false vehicle markings, phony headquarters and officers posing as generals, all meant to feed false information to enemy agents and civilians.
The 406th Engineer Combat Company guarded the perimeter, used bulldozers to make fake tank tracks and gun positions, and at times impersonated military police.
Many members, especially in the 603rd, were recruited from art schools, advertising agencies and other creative or technical fields.
claims.notes: S22 says art student Bernie Bluestein saw a recruiting notice at his Cleveland art school in March 1943, but S22 was seen only via search excerpt.

claims.claim: Four members of the 23rd landed on D-Day, and two became casualties while building false beach landing sites.
claims.notes: Congressional finding. No independent corroboration was found in this pass.

claims.claim: Lt. Fred Fox's radio operators, assigned to the cancelled Operation Troutfly, were instead attached to the 82nd Airborne, which had lost 95 percent of its radio equipment.
claims.notes: Congressional finding.

claims.claim: The 23rd's battlefield deception began in France on June 14, 1944, when Task Force Mason, a 16-man detachment under 1st Lt. Bernard Mason, set up dummy artillery to draw fire away from the 980th Field Artillery Battalion.
claims.notes: Congressional finding.

claims.claim: Operation Elephant (July 1-4, 1944) covered the 2nd Armored Division's move into the line. PL 117-85 calls it the first of 21 full-scale tactical deceptions.
claims.notes: The Fox history lists ELEPHANT as 1-4 July 1944.

claims.claim: Sources give different totals for the 23rd's deception operations: about 20 (AP), 21 full-scale (PL 117-85), 22 (National WWII Museum 2020; Luxembourg government), and 'more than 20' (National WWII Museum 2024; Smithsonian). The Fox official history names about 23 entries, but these include a rehearsal in England (CABBAGE) and an operation that never materialized (VASELINE).
claims.notes: The count depends on how rehearsals, cancelled and minor operations are counted. On screen, use 'more than 20' or 'about two dozen'.

claims.claim: Operations BRITTANY (9-12 Aug 1944) and BREST (20-27 Aug 1944) supported Allied operations in Brittany, including the siege of Brest.
claims.notes: Dates come from the Fox history transcription. The museum article mentions 'aid to the siege of Brest (summer 1944)'.

claims.claim: At Brest, the unit used visual, sonic and radio deception together for the first time. It tried to help persuade German Gen. Ramcke to surrender, which did not succeed, though it drew German attention to the flanks.
claims.notes: Single nonprofit source; the effect is an interpretation. The same page says Ramcke had about 38,000 troops, not the estimated 21,000, and that five tanks of the 709th Tank Battalion were lost near the deception area. Verify before using.

claims.claim: In Operation BETTEMBOURG (mid-to-late September 1944, Luxembourg), about 500 men impersonated the roughly 8,000-man 6th Armored Division to cover a thinly held stretch of Patton's Third Army line.
claims.notes: Start date is 14 Sept (Fox) or 15 Sept (Legacy Project). AP describes filling a gap in Patton's line 'near Metz' for eight days in September 1944, and the museum mentions holding a gap during the Metz assault. These most likely describe the same operation, but that is not stated explicitly.

claims.claim: Most of the unit was housed in a building in Limpertsberg, Luxembourg City, from September 25 to December 22, 1944. The Luxembourg government says more than a third of the unit's 22 missions took place in Luxembourg.
claims.notes: '22 missions' is the Luxembourg government's count (see C23).

claims.claim: During the Battle of the Bulge, the 23rd broadcast fake radio traffic suggesting movements of Patton's Third Army toward besieged Bastogne.
claims.notes: Congressional finding. The Fox history lists an Operation KODAK on 22-23 Dec 1944 but this pass did not confirm it is the same action.

claims.claim: The costliest operation, in which the unit simulated the 80th Infantry Division, cost 2 killed and 15 wounded. The Fox history records this casualty toll for Operation BOUZONVILLE (11-13 March 1945).
claims.notes: The museum names the simulated division and the Fox history names the operation. Linking the two relies on the matching casualty figures.

claims.claim: In total, three soldiers of the 23rd were killed and dozens wounded.
claims.notes: PL 117-85 finding; CBS cites the Ghost Army Legacy Project.

claims.claim: Operation VIERSEN (March 18-24, 1945) was the 23rd's last and largest deception. It impersonated two U.S. divisions (the 30th and 79th Infantry Divisions) to draw German forces away from the Ninth Army's real Rhine crossing.
claims.notes: Division names come from the museum; PL 117-85 says 'two complete divisions'.

claims.claim: For Viersen the unit simulated more than 30,000 troops using about 600 inflatable dummies, along with fabricated radio nets, sound recordings and real vehicles.
claims.notes: The 30,000 figure (S5) and the 600 dummies (S4) come from museum sources. PL 117-85 says only 'hundreds of inflatable and real vehicles'. A search excerpt suggested an earlier bill draft used 40,000, but this was not verified. Present the numbers as approximate.

claims.claim: Ninth Army commander Lt. Gen. William H. Simpson commended the unit after Viersen.
claims.notes: The text of the commendation was not retrieved.

claims.claim: The PL 117-85 findings quote a postwar official Army assessment that begins: "Rarely, if ever, has there been a group of such a few men" (the assessment goes on to describe the group's outsized influence on a major campaign).
claims.notes: The quoted fragment was extracted from govinfo text; re-verify it against the PDF before showing it on screen. The original document's date and author are unclear (see uncertainties). Speaker Johnson read the assessment at the ceremony.

claims.claim: The 3133rd Signal Service Company operated in Italy in 1945. In April 1945 it carried out Operation Craftsman, supporting Operation Second Wind against the Gothic Line north of Florence, working with British decoy specialists.
claims.notes: Congressional finding plus museum.

claims.claim: The 3133rd had about 200 soldiers and conducted two deceptions in Italy. It served 19 days in combat, earned a campaign star for the Po Valley campaign, and lost almost 70 percent of its 35 dummy tanks to German artillery fire.
claims.notes: About 200 men is from AP; the other details are from the museum (single source each).

claims.claim: After the war the unit's records were classified and its story was largely unknown. A few newspaper articles appeared in August 1945, and then little appeared publicly until an April 1985 Smithsonian magazine article illustrated by veteran Arthur Shilstone.
claims.notes: The Library of Congress blog (S18) also cites a New York Times article dated December 5, 1945. Use 'little' rather than 'nothing' for the postwar silence.

claims.claim: Capt. Fred Fox wrote the unit's Official History in September 1945. It is held at the National Archives (Archives II, College Park, Md.) in Record Group 407.
claims.notes: The NARA location is given by the Legacy Project transcription. It was not confirmed in the NARA catalog in this pass because the catalog API returned nothing.

claims.claim: Sources give different dates for declassification: 1996 (most sources, including the National WWII Museum, AP and the Legacy Project), 1993 (army.mil, Fort Leonard Wood), 'mid-1990s' (National WWII Museum exhibit text), 'more than 40 years' after the war (PL 117-85) and 'more than 50 years' (Speaker's release).
claims.notes: 1996 is the majority date and is tied to the Fox history. A search excerpt said the Legacy Project describes a partial declassification around 1985 followed by reclassification; this was not verified. Recommended on-screen wording: 'not fully declassified until the mid-1990s'.

claims.claim: Many veterans kept silent about their service for decades. AP reported that the son of Capt. Oscar Seale learned only after his father's 2001 death that he had served in the unit.
claims.notes: The Seale case is a single family's account reported by AP.

claims.claim: Painter Ellsworth Kelly was inducted on January 1, 1943, joined the 603rd Engineer Camouflage Battalion at Fort Meade in March 1943, and joined the 23rd at Camp Forrest in January 1944. He served in England, France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Germany and was discharged on October 23, 1945.
claims.notes: The Kelly Foundation chronology also says he produced camouflage instruction posters designed by Col. Homer Saint-Gaudens.

claims.claim: Fashion designer Bill Blass served in the 603rd Engineer Camouflage Battalion of the Ghost Army.
claims.notes: Enlistment year is given as 1942 or 1943 in secondary sources; avoid it. A widely repeated Blass quote about inflating dummy tanks was not verified from a primary source; do not use it.

claims.claim: Wildlife artist Arthur Singer (1917-1990) served in the 603rd Camouflage Engineers. His wartime watercolors appear in the Ghost Army documentary and book.
claims.notes: RIT Press says he entered the Army in 1944; other secondary sources say 1942. Avoid the date. Later fame (state birds and flowers stamps, 1982) is from secondary search results only.

claims.claim: Photographer Art Kane also served with the 603rd and went on to a successful postwar career.
claims.notes: Single museum source.

claims.claim: Shortly after D-Day, two French civilians on bicycles reportedly got past the perimeter and saw four soldiers lifting what looked like a 40-ton Sherman tank. Veteran Arthur Shilstone later painted the scene and recalled telling them the Americans were very strong.
claims.notes: This is a veteran's recollection recorded decades later and illustrated by the veteran himself. Present it as a story veterans told, not documented fact. Details vary between tellings. Seen only via search excerpts.

claims.claim: Bills titled the 'Ghost Army Congressional Gold Medal Act' were introduced in the 114th, 115th, 116th and 117th Congresses, starting with H.R. 2170 in 2015.
claims.notes: AP describes nearly a decade of advocacy by families and filmmaker Rick Beyer (S11).

claims.claim: S. 1404 became Public Law 117-85 (136 Stat. 11), approved February 1, 2022, and signed by President Joe Biden.
claims.notes: Senate passage on Dec 15, 2021 and House passage on Jan 19, 2022 were seen only in a secondary bill-tracker excerpt (Congress.gov blocked automated access). Verify on Congress.gov before stating them.

claims.claim: The Act directs that the single gold medal go to the Smithsonian Institution for display and research. It expresses the sense of Congress that the medal be displayed elsewhere, especially at places connected to the units, and authorizes bronze duplicates for sale.
claims.notes: Whether and where the Smithsonian currently displays the medal was not confirmed.

claims.claim: The Congressional Gold Medal was presented on March 21, 2024, in Emancipation Hall of the U.S. Capitol, with House Speaker Mike Johnson presiding.
claims.notes: Other speakers per S10: McConnell, Jeffries, Rep. Ann Kuster, Sens. Ed Markey and Susan Collins, and former Rep. Chris Stewart.

claims.claim: Three of the seven then-known surviving veterans attended the ceremony: Bernard Bluestein (100), John Christman (99) and Seymour Nussenbaum (100).
claims.notes: Ages are as of March 2024. The number of surviving veterans as of October 2026 is unknown; do not state it.

claims.claim: At the ceremony, Army Secretary Christine Wormuth said many of the unit's techniques are still used today.
claims.notes: Paraphrase.

claims.claim: Estimates that the Ghost Army saved 15,000 to 30,000 American lives are widely repeated but not documented. Speaker Johnson gave that range in his ceremony remarks, while the Speaker's press release says about 30,000. CBS attributes the range to 'the U.S. Army' without citing a document, and a Smithsonian magazine article repeats it. PL 117-85 gives no number, saying only that the units saved lives, and the National WWII Museum says 'thousands'.
claims.notes: No primary study or Army document behind the range was found. On screen, attribute it: 'one estimate cited by the Speaker of the House...'. Do not present it as fact.

claims.claim: The U.S. Mint's medal design shows the four deception methods on the obverse: a telegraph operator, a soldier applying a fake unit patch, a loudspeaker half-track and soldiers carrying an inflatable tank. The reverse shows the emblems of the 23rd and the 3133rd with a dedication laid out like a telegram. Designers include Justin Kunz, John P. McGraw and Phebe Hemphill.
claims.notes: Bronze duplicates were issued in 2024 in 3-inch and 1.5-inch sizes.

claims.claim: The Ghost Army (23rd Headquarters Special Troops) was a different organization from the fictitious First U.S. Army Group (FUSAG) of the British-led Operation Fortitude. The 23rd's battlefield deceptions were tactical and took place in Europe from June 1944 to March 1945.
claims.notes: Popular media often conflate the two. The museum says Ingersoll conceived the unit while working on Fortitude, and the Fox history lists a rehearsal (CABBAGE, 29 May-3 June 1944) in England. No authoritative source fetched here explicitly addresses the conflation, so frame it carefully.

claims.claim: After Germany's surrender, the 23rd helped run displaced-persons camps; the Fox history cites up to about 100,000 people in 13 camps.
claims.notes: Single primary-document source (transcription); treat the numbers as approximate.

claims.claim: Veteran Seymour Nussenbaum studied art at the Pratt Institute before the war and landed on Omaha Beach about two weeks after D-Day.
claims.notes: Personal recollection reported by AP and CBS.

claims.claim: The Library of Congress Veterans History Project holds an interview with Ghost Army member Elmer Mellebrand that discusses false equipment and sonic deception.
claims.notes: The interview itself was not viewed; the details come from the LOC blog.

claims.claim: Filmmaker Rick Beyer produced the 2013 documentary 'The Ghost Army', which aired on PBS, and co-authored the 2015 book 'The Ghost Army of World War II' with Elizabeth Sayles. Beyer is president of the Ghost Army Legacy Project.
claims.notes: The documentary and book are copyrighted secondary works and should not be reused without license.

claims.claim: Memorials in Europe include a Ghost Army marker at Bettembourg, Luxembourg, and a monument unveiled on September 7, 2023, in Limpertsberg, Luxembourg City, by the U.S. Embassy, local historians and the Ghost Army Legacy Project.
claims.notes: A Legacy Project marker near Brest, France was mentioned only in search excerpts and was not verified.

claims.claim: The National WWII Museum premiered its exhibition 'Ghost Army: The Combat Con Artists of World War II' in 2020; the exhibition later traveled to other U.S. venues.

timeline.event: Ellsworth Kelly inducted into the Army; joins the 603rd Engineer Camouflage Battalion at Fort Meade in March 1943.
Art student Bernie Bluestein sees a recruiting notice at his Cleveland art school (per Smithsonian, via search excerpt).
23rd Headquarters Special Troops activated at Camp Forrest, Tennessee, under Col. Harry L. Reeder.
3132nd and 3133rd Signal Service Companies activated at Pine Camp, NY (months per PL 117-85; Fort Drum article says March for both).
Operation CABBAGE, a rehearsal in England (Fox history).
D-Day: four members land; two become casualties building false beach landing sites.
Task Force Mason (16 men) arrives in Normandy; first secret deception in France.
Operation ELEPHANT covers the 2nd Armored Division.
Remainder of the 23rd arrives in France.
Operation BRITTANY.
Operation BREST, the first combined use of visual, sonic and radio deception (per the Legacy Project).
Operation BETTEMBOURG (Luxembourg): about 500 men impersonate the 6th Armored Division.
Most of the unit is housed in Limpertsberg, Luxembourg City.
Battle of the Bulge: fake radio traffic suggests Third Army movements toward Bastogne.
Operation BOUZONVILLE (simulating the 80th Infantry Division per the museum); 2 killed, 15 wounded.
Operation VIERSEN: two divisions impersonated to cover the Ninth Army's Rhine crossing; final operation of the 23rd.
3133rd conducts Operation Craftsman in Italy, supporting the Gothic Line breakthrough (Operation Second Wind).
Capt. Fred Fox completes the Official History of the 23rd Headquarters Special Troops.
A few newspaper articles mention the unit; the story then largely disappears.
Smithsonian magazine publishes the first feature-length public account, illustrated by veteran Arthur Shilstone.
Unit records declassified.
PBS documentary 'The Ghost Army' (Rick Beyer).
First Ghost Army Congressional Gold Medal Act bill (H.R. 2170, 114th Congress); Beyer and Sayles book published.
National WWII Museum exhibition 'Ghost Army: The Combat Con Artists of World War II' opens.
Ghost Army Congressional Gold Medal Act becomes Public Law 117-85.
Ghost Army monument unveiled in Limpertsberg, Luxembourg City.
Congressional Gold Medal presented in Emancipation Hall; three surviving veterans attend.
U.S. Mint issues Ghost Army bronze duplicate medals.

uncertainties: Lives saved: no primary Army study supporting the 15,000-30,000 figure was found. It is attributed variously to the Speaker of the House, 'the U.S. Army' (CBS) and Smithsonian magazine, while the Speaker's own press release says about 30,000. PL 117-85 gives no number.

Declassification date: 1996 (majority) vs 1993 (army.mil) vs 'mid-1990s'. Congress says classified for 'more than 40 years', the Speaker 'more than 50 years'. A possible partial declassification and reclassification around 1985 was mentioned only in a search excerpt.
Number of operations: 20, 21, 22, 'more than 20', or about 23 named entries in the Fox history, depending on how rehearsals and cancelled operations are counted.

Provenance of the 'Rarely, if ever...' assessment quoted by Congress: the Speaker said the declassified Army report appeared about 30 years after the war and is normally held at Fort Leavenworth, and the Legacy Project attributes the comment to an Army analyst decades later. The original document, author and date were not verified.

Viersen scale: more than 30,000 simulated troops and about 600 inflatables are museum figures, while the statute says only 'hundreds' of vehicles. An earlier bill draft may have said 40,000 (unverified).
Activation months of the 3132nd and 3133rd (March and June vs both March 1944).
Enlistment years for Bill Blass (1942 vs 1943) and Arthur Singer (1942 vs 1944) differ among secondary sources.
Whether the Smithsonian currently displays the Congressional Gold Medal, and where, was not confirmed.
Number of surviving veterans as of October 2026 is unknown (seven were known in March 2024).
The bicyclists and 'lifted Sherman' anecdote rests on veteran recollection, so present it as oral history.
Exact Senate and House passage dates of S. 1404 (Dec 15, 2021 and Jan 19, 2022) were seen only via a secondary bill tracker because Congress.gov blocked automated access.
Brest outcome details (Ramcke's actual troop strength, 709th Tank Battalion losses) come from a single nonprofit source.
The relationship to Operation Fortitude and FUSAG: the units were separate organizations, but no authoritative source fetched here explicitly corrects the common conflation.

Smithsonian magazine pages (2022 Gormly and the 2013-era article) could not be fetched directly (HTTP 403). Their content was seen only through search excerpts and should be re-checked before quoting.
The NARA catalog entry for RG 407 SPHQ-23 was not confirmed directly; the location comes from the Legacy Project transcription.

suggested_chapters.title: Cold open: Rubber tanks on the Rhine
suggested_chapters.summary: March 1945: an army that isn't there draws German attention away from the Ninth Army's real Rhine crossing. Pose the question: who were these men, and why did it take 50 years to hear about them?

suggested_chapters.title: An army of artists
suggested_chapters.summary: Ingersoll's idea, activation at Camp Forrest, Col. Reeder, about 1,100 men, and recruiting from art schools and ad agencies, including future names such as Ellsworth Kelly, Bill Blass, Arthur Singer and Art Kane.

suggested_chapters.title: The toolkit: sight, sound, radio and theater
suggested_chapters.summary: Inflatable decoys, Bell Labs sound trucks and wire recordings, spoof radio and the Morse 'fist', fake patches, phony generals and bulldozed tank tracks.

suggested_chapters.title: Normandy to Brittany
suggested_chapters.summary: D-Day casualties, Task Force Mason, Operation Elephant, and the Brittany and Brest operations. Include the bicyclists story, labelled as a veteran's recollection.

suggested_chapters.title: Luxembourg and the Bulge
suggested_chapters.summary: Bettembourg's phantom 6th Armored Division, the Limpertsberg base, and fake radio traffic during the Battle of the Bulge.

suggested_chapters.title: The last show: Viersen, and Italy
suggested_chapters.summary: The costly Bouzonville operation, Viersen and Simpson's commendation, the 3133rd in Italy, and the human cost.

suggested_chapters.title: Fifty years of silence
suggested_chapters.summary: Fox's 1945 history, classification, the 1985 Smithsonian article, the disputed declassification date, and families who never knew.

suggested_chapters.title: Myth vs record
suggested_chapters.summary: Separate the Ghost Army from FUSAG/Fortitude, explain why counts of operations differ, and examine where the '15,000-30,000 lives' figure comes from.

suggested_chapters.title: Gold medal at last
suggested_chapters.summary: Advocacy since 2015, PL 117-85, the March 21, 2024 ceremony with three centenarian-age veterans, the medal's design, memorials in Luxembourg, and the museum exhibition.
